status: One additive bounded constitutional/public-decision knowledge claim, original untested teaching guide and one source-fit association. No existing claim, age context or edge is changed; no actual legal determination, pupil attainment or publication is inferred.

newCard.subject: Personal & Social Development
newCard.name: Government duty to consult Indigenous peoples in Canada
newCard.description: Explain the federal/provincial Crown’s constitutional duty to meaningfully consult affected Indigenous rights-holding groups when contemplated government action may adversely affect potential or established Aboriginal or treaty rights it knows or could reasonably know about, and to accommodate where appropriate. Use supplied cases to recognise when the duty may apply, distinguishing it from ordinary public opinion gathering without deciding a real legal claim.
evidence: Explain that the duty concerns the federal/provincial government and Indigenous rights-holding groups, including First Nations, Métis and Inuit where the relevant rights/impact conditions exist. It is a legal obligation relating to rights, not merely asking all nearby residents for an optional opinion.

Given plausible original scenarios with government action, credible potential or established rights the government knows or could reasonably know about, and a supported possible adverse impact explicitly supplied, explain why the duty may apply. For an incomplete case identify missing facts; ethnicity, proximity, a municipal border or the nearest reserve alone does not decide it.

Explain timely two-way information/listening and responsive consideration of concerns before the decision, with appropriate accommodation such as changing a proposed design to avoid or reduce harm. Do not treat one meeting as automatically adequate, consultation as automatic project approval or an unconditional universal veto, or delegated developer paperwork as removing the Crown’s ultimate responsibility.
newCard.assessmentPrompt: A government is considering a fictional project and knows it could affect an Indigenous community’s stated harvesting rights. Can {{name}} explain why it may have a duty to consult and what meaningful consultation and possible accommodation are for? Change the case: if the rights or possible impact facts are missing, what would they need to know rather than just choosing the nearest reserve?

pedagogy.summary: Teach one bounded Canadian constitutional/public-decision relationship through supplied facts and explicit limits, rather than equating it with generic respect, public surveys or personal permission.
bestPractices: Keep government action, its knowledge of credible rights and possible adverse impact connected.
Use plain fictional cases with the legally relevant facts supplied; do not ask children to determine actual title or consultation adequacy.
Separate timely responsive consultation and appropriate accommodation from a guaranteed outcome or meeting-count formula.
keyRepresentations: Clearly fictional First Nation/Métis/Inuit scenario cards with supplied facts
A contrast between general public input, personal permission and the Crown duty
commonMisconceptions: Only a proven treaty claim can be relevant, or any unsupported assertion automatically triggers the duty.
The nearest reserve or an Indigenous person living nearby automatically identifies the affected rights-holding group.
A general survey or one meeting automatically completes the duty.
Consultation means automatic project approval or an unconditional universal veto.
A developer’s paperwork removes ultimate Crown responsibility.

learn.summary: Learn the basic duty and explain when it may apply in supplied credible cases, with meaningful responsiveness and appropriate accommodation rather than a legal verdict.

activities.title: Explain a rights-related government consultation duty
learnerActions: Adult setup: prepare original short summaries of the selected current federal/provincial guidance with source/date and scope labels. Explain Crown as the government acting in this public-decision context, not only a king personally asking questions. Use plain language for rights-holding groups and potential/established Aboriginal or treaty rights; no full legal text or section-number recall is required.

Teach the basic relationship: a government is considering action, knows or could reasonably know about an established right or a credible potential claim, and the action may adversely affect that right or its exercise. For example, a proposed approval might affect access to a harvesting area. Mere proximity, identity or unsupported speculation is not a complete explanation; the adult-prepared scenario provides a plausible right/impact basis, not a new legal title claim.

Original fictional Case A — First Nation: a federal agency is considering authorising work in a river. In this made-up packet, an affected First Nation has an established fishing right and the agency has received that information. A supplied project study identifies a plausible risk that the work could restrict access during the harvesting season. Explain which action/right/knowledge/possible-impact facts make consultation potentially relevant; do not decide an actual project or community’s rights.

Original fictional Case B — Métis: a province is considering approving a forest road. The teaching packet stipulates a credible, not-yet-finally-determined Métis harvesting-rights claim, with maps and specific concerns already in government files. A supplied study explains how the proposed seasonal closure could restrict exercise of that claimed right. Explain why a court judgment is not automatically required before consultation may arise, without treating any unsupported assertion as sufficient.

Original fictional Case C — Inuit: a federal agency is considering a permit for marine survey work. In this made-up scenario, an Inuit group holds an established harvesting right under a supplied agreement, and the agency has that agreement. The scenario’s study identifies a plausible adverse effect on the group’s access to the harvest during the proposed work. Explain the potentially relevant duty and what timely information/response or appropriate design/timing changes might seek to address; no outcome is guaranteed.

Original incomplete Contrast D — nearby residents: the only facts supplied are that a government is planning visitor-centre work, an Indigenous family lives nearby, and a general neighbourhood survey is proposed. No credible rights information or possible adverse rights impact is provided. Explain what is missing before identifying this particular Crown duty; residence/identity and a survey alone do not establish it. Do not conclude that no other legal obligation could exist.

Contrast a general public-opinion survey, a child seeking field-trip permission and the Crown’s rights-related duty. General public input and respectful local permissions can matter, but they do not by themselves fulfil or define this particular constitutional relationship. A missing trigger fact means more information is needed, not proof that no other legal obligation exists.

Explain meaningful consultation as timely sharing and receiving information, listening and responding to affected groups’ concerns before the decision. Discuss an explicitly supplied possible design/schedule change to avoid or reduce harm as one accommodation option where appropriate. Do not decide a real project’s adequacy, promise the requested outcome or imply that a meeting count automatically satisfies the duty.

Retain ultimate Crown responsibility even when a developer is asked to do procedural work such as providing information. Distinguish consultation from automatic permission to proceed and from a universal veto claim; the actual decision/rights/legal context matters. No real legal outcome or final consent determination is made by this task.

Remove the completed explanation key and ask the learner to explain the relationship in their own words using a changed supplied case. Change one relevant fact—government action/knowledge, credible rights basis or possible impact—and ask what would need checking. Preserve the distinction between insufficient information and an invented legal conclusion.

Offer a further fictional project/context and identify the affected rights relationship from its supplied evidence rather than carrying over one place’s names or assuming the nearest reserve is the right group. Assess explanation and limits, not a political opinion, legal vocabulary speed, personal identity disclosure, participation in a ceremony or actual external consultation.
activities.intendedInsight: This duty links contemplated government conduct with possible adverse impacts on Indigenous rights; it is a specific legal relationship, not merely a polite conversation or an automatic project outcome.
feedback: Ask which supplied action/right/impact facts support the explanation.
If a fact is missing, identify the information needed instead of making a real legal decision.
Return to meaningful information/response and the government’s ultimate responsibility if a survey, meeting count or developer letter is treated as sufficient by itself.
activities.rationale: Original untested teaching design; official factual-source review is not intervention-efficacy evidence.
sourceClaims: Federal contemplated conduct and possible adverse impacts on potential/established rights require consultation and, where appropriate, accommodation before decision/implementation.
The provincial Crown obligation involves information and response, listening and addressing adverse impacts; delegated procedural tasks do not remove ultimate Crown responsibility.

The duty concerns contemplated executive conduct, potential/established rights known to the Crown and possible adverse impacts; its meaningful scope varies with circumstances and accommodation is conditional.

constraints: The fixed introductory repertoire concerns the federal/provincial Crown duty, credible potential/established Indigenous rights, possible adverse impact, meaningful consultation and accommodation where appropriate. Additional fictional cases vary the context without changing the rule.

Teaching cases concern executive/project-approval action, not an exhaustive constitutional test or a blanket rule about lawmaking. The separate statutory consult/cooperate obligations on legislative/regulatory initiatives are not silently equated with this duty.

No real title, rights-holder status, municipal-duty issue, consultation adequacy, consent/veto dispute or required accommodation outcome is adjudicated. Other rights and legal obligations may also matter; the learner does not decide them from this basic task.

The adult supplies plausible/credible relevant facts. The task does not infer rights from ethnicity, a current reserve or geographic closeness, demand a child’s own community/identity, or fabricate a real Nation’s history.

No universal meeting count, full case-law/protocol inventory, treaty-history repertoire, section-number recital or new hard gate to generic vocabulary, personal consent or territory-map mastery. No cultural reenactment, real project action or learner-state decision.

Government knowledge can include what it could reasonably know, not only an explicit admission. The teaching packet supplies that basis; the learner is not asked to adjudicate constructive knowledge in a real case.

Cases A–D are original, clearly fictional teaching facts. The cited official guidance supports the legal relationship, not invented authentic community testimony or a claim that these events or agreements actually occurred.
reviewNotes: 2026-11-11: original bounded knowledge curation after whole-claim comparison with Australian investigation permission, Canadian territory/treaty history, local governance, community/general rights, rules/laws and civic action. Selected complete official bodies checked with limits retained; original teaching efficacy remains untested.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A government is considering a fictional project and knows it could affect an Indigenous community’s stated harvesting rights. Can {{name}} explain why it may have a duty to consult and what meaningful consultation and possible accommodation are for? Change the case: if the rights or possible impact facts are missing, what would they need to know rather than just choosing the nearest reserve?
assess.correctAnswer: Connects the supplied Crown action/knowledge, credible rights basis and possible adverse impact to a meaningful consultation obligation and appropriate accommodation; distinguishes ordinary opinion/permission and explains missing facts without deciding a real legal outcome.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A government/right-impact contrast distinguishes this particular knowledge from generic kindness or asking permission. Changed and incomplete cases expose nearest-reserve and automatic-trigger rules, while a developer/meeting-count near miss checks responsibility and meaningful response rather than memorised consultation vocabulary.
probeDeeper: What action is the government considering, what relevant right or credible claim does it know about, and what possible harm is supplied? In an incomplete case, which facts are missing and what should we avoid claiming?
Would simply asking everyone in the area or counting one meeting establish that the duty was met? Why not?
What might an appropriate response or accommodation aim to avoid or reduce, without promising a specific outcome?
If some procedural work is delegated, who retains ultimate responsibility?

errorPatterns.pattern: Substitutes generic politeness, proximity or any unverified assertion for the government/right-impact relationship.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses the nearest reserve or says any public survey is the same duty.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the explicit government action/knowledge, credible right and possible impact facts; identify missing evidence.

errorPatterns.pattern: Turns consultation into a fixed meeting count, automatic project approval or unconditional veto.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says one meeting settles adequacy or guarantees the proposed outcome.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explain timely responsive information/listening and accommodation where appropriate, retaining the actual legal/decision limits.

errorPatterns.pattern: Moves ultimate legal responsibility entirely to a private developer.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says government has no remaining responsibility because a company sent information.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish delegated procedural work from the Crown’s retained duty.

responseLevels.gap: Only generic permission/respect or an unsupported automatic rule, without the government/right-impact link.
responseLevels.partial: Recognises some consultation facts but confuses credibility/impact, meaningful response, accommodation or responsibility.
responseLevels.full: Explains the complete bounded relationship and limits across supplied changed cases, without turning missing facts into a real legal judgment.

closestCandidates.mismatch: Actual whole claim concerns a learner’s Australian Country/Place investigation, local permissions and cultural protocols. It is not the Canadian Crown’s constitutional obligation when its own conduct may harm potential/established rights. Preserve every AU requirement.
Resource-based territory/treaty/reserve identification does not explain the government decision/right-impact duty; no whole territory claim or personal-location disclosure is a necessary hard gate.
Particular1780–1850 treaty commitments/effects and wampum chronology are different historical knowledge. Do not broaden the ID into current constitutional doctrine.
Ontario authority/services and MNO representation/consultation roles do not establish the Crown’s legal trigger/responsibility, meaningful response and conditional accommodation.
Knowing law/rule distinctions and statutory/common-law origins does not identify this particular Canadian constitutional obligation.
General community respect/safety rights do not supply the particular collective-rights/government relationship.
The approved selected general protections/federal voting repertoire deliberately excludes this distinct section35 relationship. Preserve it rather than silently expand.
Citizen petitions/campaigns and shared civic goals are not the government’s duty to rights-holding groups.

actions: Teach and assess the complete bounded card and original guide, including its three actual original fictional FN/Métis/Inuit cases and incomplete nearby-resident contrast. The official sources support the rule; none of these invented events is represented as real community testimony.

Require the child to explain the federal/provincial government action, known or reasonably knowable credible potential/established right and possible adverse impact in the supplied case. Mere identity, distance, survey attendance or unsupported speculation is not a completed explanation.

Explain timely meaningful information/listening/response and accommodation where appropriate, retaining Crown responsibility, decision/adequacy limits and uncertainty. A changed or incomplete case tests transfer without deciding actual rights, the required outcome or a real legal dispute.

limits: The existing Australian Country investigation-permission, Canadian territory/treaty history, local-governance, generic rights and selected Canadian general-rights claims remain unchanged. This particular public-decision relationship is independently assessed.
Executive/project-scenario scope is not an exhaustive case-law course or a universal rule about legislation, municipalities, consent or private legal disputes. Other obligations may matter.
The original guide is a source-checked authoring design with low teaching-efficacy confidence, not a classroom study or inferred learner mastery.
